question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Administrative differences between European powers in India]
options: English EIC – Joint-stock company with Court of Directors in London overseeing Indian operations
Portuguese Estado da India – Crown-controlled administration headed by Viceroy at Goa
Dutch VOC – Governed by 'Heeren XVII' (Board of 17 Directors) based in Amsterdam
French Compagnie des Indes – Fully private company with no French royal involvement or control
wrong_fact: The French Compagnie des Indes was NOT a fully private company. It was established under royal patronage by Jean-Baptiste Colbert in 1664 with heavy state involvement, royal funding, and government direction. The French state had significant control — unlike the EIC which started as a private joint-stock company. The French company was essentially a state-sponsored enterprise.
explanation: The EIC was a joint-stock company (from 1600) with the Court of Directors in London overseeing Indian Presidencies. The Portuguese Estado da India was a direct Crown operation, with the Viceroy at Goa representing the Portuguese King. The Dutch VOC was governed by the Heeren XVII (literally 'Lords Seventeen'), a board drawn from the six VOC chambers across the Netherlands. The French Compagnie des Indes (1664) was state-sponsored and state-directed — Colbert set it up with royal capital — NOT a private company.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Administrative structures across European settlements in India]
options: English Presidency – Three-tier: Governor, Council, and subordinate factories
Dutch VOC in India – Governed locally by a Director-General at Batavia with Indian settlements as subordinate
Portuguese – Viceroy at Goa with Captains (Capitãos) heading subsidiary fortresses like Diu and Daman
French – Conseil Supérieur (Superior Council) at Pondicherry replaced by Governor-General as independent body
wrong_fact: The Conseil Supérieur at Pondicherry did not replace the Governor-General as an independent body — the Governor-General (or Director-General) remained the supreme authority. The Conseil Supérieur was an advisory and judicial body subordinate to the Governor of Pondicherry, not an independent replacement. The French administration became increasingly dependent on Paris and was never structured as a self-governing independent council superseding the Governor.
explanation: English Presidencies had a hierarchical structure: Governor with a Council at the top, with subordinate factories (like Masulipatnam under Madras). The Dutch VOC's Indian settlements were subordinate to the Governor-General at Batavia (Jakarta). Portuguese administration had Captains commanding subsidiary fortresses at Diu, Daman, Bassein, etc. The French Conseil Supérieur at Pondicherry was an advisory/judicial council under the Governor, not an independent body — option D misrepresents its role.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Key administrative landmarks differentiating British governance from other Europeans]
options: Regulating Act (1773) – Brought EIC under British Parliamentary oversight for the first time
Pitt's India Act (1784) – Created Board of Control in London to oversee EIC's political functions
Charter Act (1833) – Made Governor-General of Bengal into Governor-General of India; EIC lost its trading monopoly
Charter Act (1813) – Ended EIC's monopoly over ALL Indian trade including tea and China trade
wrong_fact: The Charter Act of 1813 ended EIC's monopoly over INDIAN trade, but specifically retained EIC's monopoly over China trade and tea trade. The China trade and tea monopoly was only abolished by the Charter Act of 1833. Option D incorrectly states the 1813 Act ended all trade monopolies including tea and China trade.
explanation: The Regulating Act (1773) was the first Parliamentary intervention in EIC affairs, creating the Governor-General of Bengal. Pitt's India Act (1784) set up the Board of Control in London for political oversight. The Charter Act (1833) made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India (Lord William Bentinck was first) and ended EIC's commercial functions entirely. The Charter Act of 1813 only threw open Indian trade to all British merchants — the China trade and tea monopoly survived until 1833.
